```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup}
# library(pitw)
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
.gg_pedantic(size = 0.5)
set.seed(1001)
```

We fixed the median and coefficient of variation of the predictive
distributions and varied the distributional family. This lets us examine
how the scores respond when a forecast uses a different shape from the
one that generated the observations. For example, a normal forecast for
a positive, skewed rate can have the same median and coefficient of
variation as a lognormal forecast.

We also compare these scores with those from changing the reported width
within one family. Finally, we examine how the scores change when we apply
a common location bias to forecasts with skewed errors.

# 1. Matching the median and coefficient of variation

The `norm4`, `lnorm4` and `gamma4` families are parametrised by a
median and a coefficient of variation $\kappa$. We use those two
parameters to match forecasts across families.

The construction uses the fact that `lnorm4` and `gamma4` are scale families.
Draw a multiplicative error $w_i \sim \mathcal{T}(\text{median}=1, \kappa)$
from the *true* family $\mathcal{T}$, and place the forecast at
$\ell_i = x/w_i$. Then

$$
x \;=\; \ell_i w_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{T}(\text{median}=\ell_i,\ \kappa)
$$

so a forecaster reporting $\mathcal{T}(\ell_i, \kappa)$ is **exactly
calibrated** by construction. A forecaster reporting a different family
$\mathcal{R}(\ell_i, \kappa)$ — same median, same coefficient of variation — is
wrong in shape and in nothing else.

```{r construction}
# One estimator: n predictions of a true value of 1, errors from `truth`,
# predictive distribution reported as `report`.
misspecified <- function(truth, report, kappa, kappa_reported = kappa,
                         bias = 1, n = 2000) {
  w <- rlang::as_function(sprintf("r%s", truth))(n, 1, kappa)
  pit_w(rep(1, n), bias / w, kappa_reported, dist = report, link = "log")
}
```

We check that each family's quantile function and cumulative distribution
function invert one another at the tested probabilities.

```{r roundtrip}
map_dfr(c("gamma4", "lnorm4", "norm4"), function(f) {
  q <- rlang::as_function(sprintf("q%s", f))(0.9, 2, 0.5)
  tibble(family = f, q90 = q,
         recovered_p = rlang::as_function(sprintf("p%s", f))(q, 2, 0.5))
})
```

When the forecast uses the generating family, the reference mean for
$B_{pit}$ at $n = 2000$ is about
`r round(sqrt(2 * pi) / 8 / sqrt(2000), 4)`. We compare this value with
the simulated scores.

```{r sanity}
map_dfr(c(0.3, 0.6, 1.0), function(k) {
  misspecified("gamma4", "gamma4", k) |> mutate(kappa = k)
}) |>
  transmute(kappa, B_pit, U_pit, D_pit)
```

# 2. Scores by predictive family

We vary $\kappa$ from 0.01 to 0.8. At the lower end the three families
have similar shapes. We use two generating families and three reported
families, with 20 replicate estimators for each combination.

```{r sweep}
grid <- crossing(
  truth  = c("gamma4", "lnorm4"),
  report = c("gamma4", "lnorm4", "norm4"),
  kappa  = c(0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8),
  rep    = 1:20
)

sweep <- grid |>
  mutate(score = pmap(list(truth, report, kappa),
                      ~ misspecified(..1, ..2, ..3))) |>
  unnest(score) |>
  mutate(match = if_else(truth == report, "correct family", "misspecified"))

summ <- sweep |>
  group_by(truth, report, kappa, match) |>
  summarise(across(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), median), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r sweep-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
crit <- tibble(
  metric = c("B_pit", "U_pit", "D_pit"),
  critical = c(b_pit_significance(NA, 2000)$critical_0.05,
               u_pit_significance(NA, 2000)$critical_0.05,
               d_pit_significance(NA, 2000)$critical_0.05)
)

summ |>
  pivot_longer(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, c("B_pit", "U_pit", "D_pit"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(kappa, value, colour = report, linetype = match)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(data = crit, aes(yintercept = critical),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = filter(crit, metric == "D_pit"),
             aes(yintercept = -critical),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ truth, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(truth = ~ paste("true family:", .x))) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("coefficient of variation  ", kappa)),
       y = NULL, colour = "reported as", linetype = NULL)
```

The scores for mismatched families began to cross the reference thresholds
around $\kappa = 0.4$ in these simulations. At $\kappa = 0.2$, the scores
shown remained within the thresholds.

The sign of $D_{pit}$ changed when we exchanged the gamma and lognormal
families. When we reported normal forecasts for either of the two skewed
generating families, $D_{pit}$ stayed near zero while $U_{pit}$ increased.
Departures on opposing sides of the distribution can cancel in the directed
score while still contributing to the undirected score.

# 3. Comparing changes in shape and width

We compare $U_{pit}/|D_{pit}|$ for mismatched families with the same
ratio for forecasts whose reported width differs within the generating
family.

```{r ratio}
width_error <- crossing(kappa_reported = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9), rep = 1:20) |>
  mutate(score = map(kappa_reported, ~ misspecified("gamma4", "gamma4", 0.6, .x))) |>
  unnest(score) |>
  transmute(scenario = "wrong width, right family", U_pit, D_pit)

shape_error <- sweep |>
  filter(match == "misspecified", kappa >= 0.6) |>
  transmute(scenario = if_else(report == "norm4",
                               "wrong skew (normal reported)",
                               "wrong tail (gamma/lnorm swapped)"),
            U_pit, D_pit)

bind_rows(width_error, shape_error) |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(median_U = median(U_pit),
            median_abs_D = median(abs(D_pit)),
            ratio = median(U_pit / abs(D_pit)))
```

```{r ratio-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
bind_rows(width_error, shape_error) |>
  ggplot(aes(abs(D_pit), U_pit, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = expression(paste("|", D[pit], "|")), y = expression(U[pit]),
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

A **pure width error sits on the diagonal**: $U_{pit} = |D_{pit}|$ almost
exactly, because stating intervals uniformly too narrow pushes the PIT values
toward both ends in a way that the signed weight accumulates rather than
cancels.

In these simulations, the tail-weight differences produced a pattern of
scores similar to that from changing the reported width. The gamma and
lognormal comparisons at matched median and $\kappa$ also sit close to the
diagonal.

A **skew mismatch sits well above the diagonal**, with ratios of 3–20. Fitting
a symmetric family to a skewed one produces a departure the signed metric
cancels, so $U_{pit} \gg |D_{pit}|$.

So the practical rule is the one the three-part test already implies, now with
a concrete cause attached:

| Pattern | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| $U_{pit} \approx \lvert D_{pit}\rvert$, both significant | net dispersion error — stated width wrong, **or** tail weight wrong |
| $U_{pit} \gg \lvert D_{pit}\rvert$ | asymmetry mismatch — a symmetric family fitted to a skewed quantity |
| only $B_{pit}$ significant | location error, family and width fine |

# 4. Bias adjustment with skewed errors

The adjustment uses the median to estimate a common shift on the link
scale. With a log link, multiplying each forecast by $b$ applies a
common location shift. We vary $b$ to see how the scores respond when the
errors are skewed.

```{r bias-invariance}
bias_sweep <- crossing(
  report = c("gamma4", "lnorm4", "norm4"),
  bias   = c(1, 1.25, 1.6, 2),
  rep    = 1:20
) |>
  mutate(score = pmap(list(report, bias),
                      ~ misspecified("gamma4", ..1, 0.6, bias = ..2))) |>
  unnest(score)

bias_sweep |>
  group_by(report, bias) |>
  summarise(across(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), median), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bias, values_from = c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit))
```

```{r bias-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
bias_sweep |>
  pivot_longer(c(B_pit, U_pit, D_pit), names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, c("B_pit", "U_pit", "D_pit"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(bias), value, colour = report, fill = report)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_boxplot(outliers = FALSE, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "multiplicative bias", y = NULL, colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

$B_{pit}$ increased with the size of the location shift. The two adjusted
scores were unchanged across the values of $b$ studied, including $b = 2$,
for all the reported families in this simulation.

# 5. Summary and caveats

- A pure family mismatch — right median, right coefficient of variation, wrong
  shape — **is** detected, from around $\kappa \approx 0.4$ upward.
- A **tail-weight** mismatch is indistinguishable from a width error, because
  it produces the same PIT values. The metrics report the net realised
  dispersion error, which is the honest answer to the question they are asked.
- A **skew** mismatch has its own signature, $U_{pit} \gg |D_{pit}|$, which no
  width error produces.
- The median-based bias adjustment remains exactly bias-invariant under skewed
  errors, including when the predictive family is simultaneously wrong.

Caveats. All of this holds the median and coefficient of variation matched exactly; a real misspecified model usually gets those slightly wrong too, so
the signatures above will be mixed rather than pure. The families compared here
are the realistic ones for positive skewed quantities, and nothing is claimed
about heavy-tailed symmetric alternatives such as a $t$ distribution, which the
package does not currently provide in the four-parameter form. And a normal
family fitted to a positive quantity places mass below zero; at the larger
$\kappa$ values here that is part of what is being detected, which is realistic
but means the effect is not purely one of skew.
